summary: Lists call flows for SIP session recording with snapshots of the metadata, for settings such as call centers and trading firms that must record calls. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Some businesses must keep a copy of every phone call. This shows example step-by-step exchanges for making that copy.

subtitle: Example call flows for recording SIP sessions with metadata

tldr.problem: Regulatory environments like call centers and trading firms must record calls for compliance and consumer protection, but implementations need guidance on how to exchange metadata about recording sessions.
tldr.mechanism: This document provides detailed call flow examples showing how a Session Recording Client sends metadata snapshots to a Session Recording Server using XML-formatted information about participants, media streams, and session state changes.
tldr.outcome: Implementers have concrete examples to follow when building session recording systems based on the SIP recording architecture defined in related RFCs.

today: RFC 8068 is an Informational document that provides normative examples for implementers of SIP session recording systems. It remains the primary reference for real-world call flow patterns in SIPREC implementations.

sections.title: Session Recording for Regulated Environments
sections.content:
Session recording is a critical requirement in many communications environments such as call centers, trading organizations, and other regulated businesses. In these settings, compliance and consumer-protection regulations often require that all calls be recorded. Session recording works by sending a copy of each media stream to a recording device. This document shows practical examples of the metadata snapshots that a Session Recording Client (SRC)—the component that initiates recording—sends to a Session Recording Server (SRS)—the device that stores and processes the recordings.

Rather than covering complete SIP and SDP message details, the examples focus on the most relevant parts and the XML metadata snapshots, making the flows easier to understand and implement.
sections.plainLanguage: Recording systems need to know who is talking, what they are sending, and what is happening to the call. This section explains why recording metadata matters.

sections.title: Metadata XML Structure and Snapshot Format
sections.content:
The metadata sent from the SRC to the SRS is XML-based and describes the recording session. A metadata snapshot includes information about the communication session (the call itself), the participants (the people or systems on the call), the media streams (the audio or video being recorded), and the associations between them.

The document shows two important snapshot modes. In datamode: complete, the snapshot contains all relevant information for setting up a new recording session. In datamode: partial, the snapshot contains only the fields that have changed since the last update, making updates efficient. For example, when a participant goes on hold, the SRC sends a partial snapshot showing which participant is no longer sending media.
sections.plainLanguage: The metadata is like a label on a filing cabinet: it says who is in the call, what audio or video is being saved, and whether someone put the call on pause.

sections.title: Basic Call Recording Scenarios
sections.content:
The document provides examples of common call scenarios. A basic call flow shows Alice and Bob in a conversation with both audio and video streams being recorded. The SRC sends an initial INVITE with a complete metadata snapshot, then sends RTP media streams to the SRS, and can update the metadata with RE-INVITE or UPDATE messages when the call state changes.

Two important call scenarios are demonstrated: hold and resume, where a participant pauses the call and later resumes it, requiring metadata updates to show which media streams are active; and call transfer, where one participant leaves and is replaced by another, requiring the SRC to send metadata showing the participant change and the new session state.
sections.plainLanguage: A basic call shows two people talking and both being recorded. Hold/resume shows what happens when one person puts the other on pause. Transfers show what happens when one person connects to someone else instead.

sections.title: Conference Recording with Mixed Streams
sections.content:
In conference scenarios, the SRC may act as a conference focus (like a bridge or multipoint control unit) that mixes multiple participant streams into a single recorded stream, or records each participant stream separately. When recording mixed streams, the metadata still tracks which participants are sending to and receiving from the mixed stream.

The document shows that mixed-stream recordings require the SRC to send multiple sipSessionID elements—one for each pair of participants joining the conference through the focus. This preserves information about which individual sessions feed into the conference being recorded.
sections.plainLanguage: In a conference call with many people, the recording system can either save each person's voice separately or mix them together. Either way, the metadata tracks who is participating.

sections.title: Call Disconnect and Session Termination
sections.content:
When participants disconnect, the SRC sends a BYE message with a metadata snapshot indicating that the session has ended. The snapshot includes a stop-time element on the session and disassociate-time elements on each participant, marking when they left the call.

The document also covers specialized scenarios such as persistent recording sessions between an SRC and SRS that continue across multiple communication sessions, and turret-case flows used on financial trading floors where multiple traders' communications are recorded into single recording sessions with mixed streams.
sections.plainLanguage: When the call ends, the recording system marks the time it stopped and notes when each person hung up.
